hints: Think about what type of oxide reacts with a base like NaOH, acidic, basic or amphoteric?
Recall that $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ are strongly acidic, so all three dissolve in cold dilute alkali.
Remember the special case of silicon dioxide with its giant covalent lattice, and consider which conditions (cold dilute vs hot concentrated) it needs to react.
walkthrough:
**Classify the oxides**

Acidic oxides react with bases to form a salt and water. Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases. Here $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ are acidic, and $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric.

Rule to use:
$$\text{acidic oxide + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{salt + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check the three that do react in the cold**

$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ dissolves in NaOH to give sodium aluminate. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ gives sodium phosphate. $\text{SO}_2$ gives sodium sulfite, even in cold dilute alkali.

Examples:
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$$
$$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 12\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 4\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Spot the exception**

$\text{SiO}_2$ is acidic in theory, but it has a very strong giant covalent lattice. It is kinetically unreactive toward cold, dilute $\text{NaOH}$.

It only reacts with hot, concentrated $\text{NaOH}$:
$$\text{SiO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH (hot, conc.)} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So under cold, dilute conditions, no salt is produced.

options.A: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is amphoteric, so it does react with cold dilute NaOH to form the salt sodium aluminate, $\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$. Students sometimes think only acids react with alkalis and forget amphoteric oxides react too.
options.B: $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is a strongly acidic Period 3 oxide and reacts readily with cold dilute NaOH to give sodium phosphate, $\text{Na}_3\text{PO}_4$. It is very soluble and reactive, so it is not the exception.
options.C: $\text{SO}_2$ is an acidic oxide and reacts easily with cold dilute NaOH to give sodium sulfite, $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$ (or $\text{NaHSO}_3$). Do not confuse it with unreactive $\text{SiO}_2$ just because both are non-metal dioxides.
options.D: $\text{SiO}_2$ does not react with cold, dilute NaOH. Although it is acidic, its giant covalent structure makes it inert under mild conditions and it needs hot, concentrated NaOH to form $\text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$. Therefore it is the oxide that produces no salt here.
